items.title: 56800_John Simmons oral history interview
items.q: Don Byers just grabbed it right away, boom. He didn't even have to go down to Minton's to get it. He heard them doing it and he started doing it, too, you know.

ctx.x: Uh-huh. So, during that time, then, after Diz came back from Los Angeles, from where we are now, he came back to New York and organized this large band, and Gil Fuller was writing for him. And they had this arrangement, "Things to Come". Now, they shouldn't have done that, really, because it was so fast and furious, that was too much to lay on

the public all at once, in such a big dose, you know. They should have eased up on the people with it. When that record came out, it scared everybody to death. People started switching from alto to baritone, everything else. It was helter skelter, really. Ben Webster tried to play it and he couldn't get into it. He'd get tied up in it and he'd get so angry he wanted to throw his horn up against the wall. But Coleman Hawkins, he went right into it. He had a piano, and he'd sit down at the piano and figure out what…
You mean that one record, 'Things to Come', or the style?
